items.title: Marian McPartland interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, April 26, 1997
items.q: Next year the kid comes back, having listened to Bill Evans or somebody, and is playing away

ctx.x: Okay. Do you think that jazz can be successfully taught — to play?

I don’t know. Sometimes I think it can. I think, well I actually did about a three-month period in the Washington, D.C. schools and we got a huge grant for this, to go around to © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

the public schools with just this thing in mind, to teach kids to play jazz. And I used all the local musicians and one of the best tunes I thought to get the kids started to play would be a blues, and then we picked “C Jam Blues” because it’s so repetitive, and the kids had these little instruments like a vibraharp, with two octaves they all had to play on. And we did in fact get kids to not only play this tune but to improvise on it. And we culminated with a concert with Duke, he came down and played with a…

items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Going down to the Vanguard and hearing Bill Evans.

ctx.x: O.k. So it wasn’t just your trio coming into Birdland. It was always one . . .

No, no, I played in jam sessions. I played in a lot of jam sessions. In fact it almost seemed as if . . . sometimes . . . if people would bend over backwards to be especially nice or . . . I don’t know. I really can say I’ve had pretty much good feelings from everybody. I can’t think of anybody that’s an enemy or somebody I have bad feelings about. Except [laughs] a bass player, the first bass player that worked with me in the Embers. I’ve just remembered him. I can’t think what his name was. Bill . . . He was a…
That can be a little disconcerting.

items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We had . . . Another Wisconsin kid, isn’t he?

ctx.x: He’s playing with Ray Brown now. Brilliant, brilliant talent. I’m partial to him.
Oh, I know. We had . . . Another Wisconsin kid, isn’t he?
